title: Forecasting Stock Market Crashes via Real-Time Recession Probabilities: A Quantum Computing Approach
abstract_summary: The paper develops and compares quantum-based forecasting methods to predict stock market crashes using real-time recession probabilities across a large multi-country sample. It evaluates Quantum Boltzmann Machines, Quantum Support Vector Regression and Quantum Neural Networks, finding QBMs achieve the highest predictive accuracy (around mid-90s percent) and identifies region-specific macroeconomic and financial predictors, with implications for early-warning systems and policy responses.
methodology_description: The study constructs a global forecasting framework to predict stock-market crashes (binary indicator) using three quantum-inspired/quantum machine-learning approaches and a sensitivity analysis for variable selection. The dependent variable is a country-level binary crash indicator CIt+1 that equals 1 when the country stock return at t+1 falls below a historical threshold defined as the 5th percentile of the 10-year rolling return distribution; otherwise 0. The input set contains 32 macroeconomic, financial, commodity and labor/open-economy predictors collected for 104 countries over 1974–2019 (sources: FRED, World Bank, IMF, S&P Global Market Intelligence). The dataset was split 70% train / 10% validation / 20% test; 500 random dataset draws were generated and cross-validated 10 times. Three modeling approaches are implemented and compared: (i) Support Vector Regression with a Quantum Bat Algorithm optimizer (SVRQBA) for parameter search; (ii) Quantum Boltzmann Machines (QBMs) trained to match data and model first- and second-order moments via gradient-based updates in a Hamiltonian formalism; and (iii) Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) that employ qubit-based representations, rotation gates and a feed-forward/backpropagation training rule. A Sobol sensitivity analysis is used to identify the most influential input variables and produce a reduced/robust model. Multi-step iterative forecasting is used for horizon extension (1-step ahead trained forecasts are appended and used to produce 2-step ahead forecasts, etc.). Performance is reported by region and globally using classification accuracy, RMSE and MAPE. Code was implemented in Python 3.8 using NumPy and Qiskit (Qiskit referenced), executed on local CPU hardware.
algorithms_used: Quantum Bat Algorithm (bat algorithm used to search/optimize SVR parameters)
experimental_setup: Local workstation (Intel Core i7-10700, 16-core) running Python 3.8; implementations used NumPy and Qiskit. Data split 70% train / 10% validation / 20% test; 500 random dataset draws and 10-fold cross-validation. Models trained per-region and globally; multi-step iterative forecasting used for horizons t+1 and t+2.
dataset_used: Country-level monthly macroeconomic, financial and market data for 104 countries spanning 1974–2019. Dependent variable: binary crash indicator defined by stock return below 5th percentile of a rolling 10-year return distribution. Independent variables: 32 predictors across Domestic Prices (e.g., CPI, VIX, S&P, NASDAQ, DAX, market capitalization, PER, consumer/business confidence), Domestic Real Macro (GDP growth, industrial production, exports, imports, trade, gross fixed capital formation), Commodities and Financial (oil and gold prices, interest rate spread, 10y government bond yields, real interest rate, federal funds rate, money aggregates), and Open Economy/Labor (real effective exchange rate, labor force, unemployment, payrolls, government consumption). Data sources: FRED, World Bank Open Data, IMF, S&P Global Market Intelligence (SNL).

experiment_input.sample_size: 104 countries (panel/monthly observations aggregated to modeling frequency used in study)
experiment_input.dependent_variable_definition: Binary crash indicator CIt+1 = 1 if ret_stock,t+1 < HRT_stock,t+1 where HRT_stock,t+1 is the 5th percentile of the stock return distribution over a 10-year rolling window; else 0.
experiment_input.preprocessing: Rolling 10-year percentile threshold calculation for crash label; standard train/validation/test split (70/10/20); 500 random dataset draws and 10-fold cross-validation. Sobol sensitivity analysis used to select/identify most influential variables. Exact additional preprocessing (e.g., missing-value treatment, scaling, stationarity transforms) not fully specified in the paper.

experiment_process.overview: Per-region and global model development and comparison using three approaches. Models trained on the training set, tuned/monitored on validation set (early stop), and evaluated on test set. Cross-validation over 500 random draws with 10-fold CV.
SVRQBA_pipeline: Formulate SVR with nonlinear kernel and epsilon-insensitive loss
Optimize SVR hyperparameters using the Bat Algorithm (frequency-based global search and local random walk steps; equations for position and velocity updates provided in paper)
Train SVR on training data, validate on validation set, test on test set
QBM_pipeline: Map variables to a quantum Hamiltonian representation H(S) with biases h_i and couplings J_ij
Train QBM with gradient-based updates to match data and model first- and second-order moments (ΔW_ij and Δb_i formulas provided); quantum effects are used to approximate model expectations
Evaluate classification performance on validation/test sets
QNN_pipeline: Encode inputs as qubit superposition states; apply parameterized rotation gates (U(Δθ))
Compute network outputs via feed-forward (classical activation functions applied to measured/decoded qubit outputs)
Train via back-propagation-like weight updates (Δw_jk = η e_k f'(v_j))
experiment_process.sensitivity_analysis: Sobol decomposition of output variance to compute first-order S_i and total sensitivity indices S_Ti; used to identify and report most influential variables per region and globally.
experiment_process.forecasting_horizon_extension: Multi-step iterative forecasting: produce t+1 forecast, append it as if actual, then forecast t+2, etc. Performance reported for t+1 and t+2.

metrics_reported: Classification accuracy (training/validation/testing per region and model)
experiment_output.performance_summary: Quantum Boltzmann Machines achieved the highest average classification accuracy across regions (~96.2% reported as average in text; per-region accuracy in tables), SVRQBA achieved ~94.6% average, QNNs achieved ~93% average. RMSE and MAPE reported per split/region. Multi-step forecasts: for horizon t+1 QBMs ≈95.92% average accuracy; for horizon t+2 QBMs ≈92.54% average accuracy.
experiment_output.baselines: Comparative evaluation across the three proposed models (SVRQBA, QBM, QNN). No external non-quantum baselines (e.g., logistic regression, random forest) explicitly reported in the results tables.

reproducibility_notes: The paper lists data sources (FRED, World Bank, IMF, S&P Global) and software libraries (Python, NumPy, Qiskit) and provides detailed model descriptions and equations. However, the authors do not provide a public code repository, the exact processed dataset (country list, exact observation counts), or hyperparameter values (e.g., SVR kernel type and C, ε; bat algorithm parameters; QBM/QNN architecture sizes), nor details of preprocessing (missing-data handling, scaling). Reproduction is possible in principle using the cited data sources and described splits/variables, but would require reimplementation and assumptions about unspecified parameters. Overall: partial reproducibility; code and processed data are not explicitly provided.

[supported] A Support Vector Regression combined with a Quantum Bat Algorithm (SVRQBA) achieved strong performance (authors report ~94.59% average by regions).
[supported] Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) performed slightly worse than QBM and SVRQBA in this study (reported test accuracies generally in the low-90s%).

results_summary: The paper compares three quantum-inspired/quantum-formulated forecasting methods (SVRQBA, Quantum Boltzmann Machines, and Quantum Neural Networks) to predict binary monthly stock market crash events across multiple world regions. QBMs achieved the best empirical predictive performance (authors report ~96.22% average regional accuracy), followed by SVRQBA (~94.59%) and QNNs (~low-90s%). The study reports favorable RMSE and MAPE values for the models, performs multi-step forecasts (t+1 and t+2) with decreasing but still high accuracy, and uses Sobol sensitivity analysis to identify key macro-financial predictors (GDP, industrial production, exports, market indices, VIX, house prices, interest rates, etc.). The authors claim policy relevance and potential early-warning applications. An internal inconsistency in reported sample size (104 vs 161 countries) is present.

quantum_advantage_detail: The paper uses quantum-formulated models (QBMs, QNNs) and quantum toolkits (Qiskit referenced) and reports higher predictive accuracy for QBM. However, there is no demonstration of a hardware quantum advantage (no runtime or resource benchmarks on quantum hardware, no comparisons of quantum vs classical implementations isolating quantum effects). The claimed benefits are therefore empirical improvements in model performance in this study but not proven as due to quantum hardware or quantum speedup.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — Quantum Boltzmann Machines (QBMs) reported the highest predictive performance (~96.2% average classification accuracy) versus Quantum SVR (SVRQBA) and QNNs across a large multi-country sample.

#idea:hybrid-approach — The study combines classical data preprocessing, Sobol sensitivity analysis, and classical training infrastructure with quantum-inspired/quantum-ML models (QBMs, QNNs, SVR with quantum bat optimizer) implemented via Qiskit and NumPy on local hardware.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Models are evaluated on extensive empirical data (104 countries, 1974–2019) with cross-validation (500 draws, 10-fold CV) and reported metrics (accuracy, RMSE, MAPE) by region and horizon (t+1, t+2).
#idea:hybrid-approach — Multi-step iterative forecasting and variable selection (Sobol) are integrated to produce reduced robust models suitable for early-warning systems and policy applications.
#limitation:simulation-only — All quantum models were implemented/executed on classical local hardware (Qiskit/NumPy on CPU); no experiments on quantum processors were reported.

#limitation:data-encoding — The paper provides a high-level description of qubit-based encodings for QNNs and Hamiltonian mapping for QBMs, but practical costs and details of encoding 32 real-valued predictors into qubit states are not fully specified.
contradictions: The paper claims quantum-model superiority (QBMs outperforming alternatives) but evaluations were performed on classical hardware/simulators and compared primarily against quantum-inspired baselines (SVRQBA, QNN). This raises a contradiction between claimed "quantum" advantage and lack of demonstration on actual quantum hardware or against strong classical ML baselines (e.g., random forests, gradient-boosted trees).

High reported accuracy on a large panel is presented without evidence that the approaches scale to real quantum devices; the simulation-only implementation and absence of discussion on qubit requirements, noise resilience or runtime scaling contradicts any implicit claims about near-term or large-scale deployability on QPUs.
